about.title: About me
about.greeting.p1: I'm a software engineer in Berlin, most at home on the backend: APIs, data models, the parts that have to keep working when nobody's watching. Before code I was a sound engineer, co-ran a club and worked on film sets, and I still build with my hands: campers, tiny houses, furniture.

about.drivesMe.label: What drives me
about.drivesMe.item1.title: Clarity & Coherence
about.drivesMe.item1.text: I like systems that are calm and logical. When something feels off, I tend to notice early.
about.drivesMe.item2.title: Human & Value Orientation
about.drivesMe.item2.text: Technology should serve people, not distract them. I try to build with that in mind.
about.drivesMe.item3.title: Learning & Doing
about.drivesMe.item3.text: I learn best by making things. Curiosity keeps me going.
about.drivesMe.item4.title: Aesthetics & Craftsmanship
about.drivesMe.item4.text: In the workshop, a wrong cut costs a board. I bring the same habit of checking before committing to code.
about.outsideScreen.title: Beyond the Screen
about.outsideScreen.p1: Outside of work I make music, ride long distances by bike and spend a lot of time in the workshop. Photography came recently, slowly and intuitively.

experience.glance.title: At a glance
experience.chapter1.title: Sound, Space, and Systems
experience.chapter1.quote: Passionate people teach their passions effortlessly, and learning works best when it's peer-to-peer and practice-based.
experience.chapter1.image.caption: Kultstätte Keller – 2014
experience.chapter1.p1: It started at 21, standing behind a mixing console at **SAE Institute** in Berlin, learning to shape acoustic space. I'd played bass in a punk band through my teens. Music was always present, but what drew me was the engineering: how frequencies interact, how a mix creates dimension, how you build atmosphere from discrete elements.
experience.chapter1.p2: **Audio production taught me a way of thinking** I didn't have words for yet. Balancing elements, finding clarity in complexity, making technical decisions that serve a feeling. After SAE, I spent time on film sets through my father's connections as a camera operator. Those productions taught me about collaboration under pressure, about craft, and about being present when the work demands it.
experience.chapter1.p3: In 2011, through friends in Berlin's cultural scene, I got involved with an empty building in Neukölln. The idea was to create space for art and community events. I started building recording studios in the basement. What we created instead was **Kultstätte Keller**, which grew from occasional parties into a nightclub running entertainment six nights a week. I never finished those studios. Instead, I became co-owner and operator, managing sound systems, technical infrastructure, and logistics for a space that had found its own momentum.
experience.chapter1.p4: Running Kultstätte taught me about systems at scale: organisational, technical, human. But by 2015, after years in nightlife, I started noticing the toll. How people age in that environment, the consumption, the feeling that something essential was missing. I wanted to build things that lasted differently.
experience.chapter1.p5: Around this time, I did a three-month internship at **Peppermint Park Studios** in Hannover, working under Hans Martin Buff, who would later win a Grammy. I learned more in those three months than in my entire formal education. Not because the curriculum was better, but because I was learning from someone deeply passionate about their craft. That planted a seed: **passionate people teach effortlessly**, and learning works best peer-to-peer.
experience.chapter1.p6: This insight became **U/skillity**, a platform I co-founded: a peer-to-peer marketplace for microskills. Airbnb, but for knowledge. The problem was I had no real understanding of business or technology beyond what I'd picked up intuitively.
experience.chapter1.p7: In 2016, I completed an **IHK certification in Business Administration** and discovered I enjoyed structured learning. At 30, with years of practical experience, formal education felt different than it had as a teenager. I wanted more.
experience.chapter1.p8: That's when I found the HEAR programme at the National University of Ireland Maynooth, a route designed for mature students entering higher education later in life. I took the entry exams, got accepted, and moved to Ireland.
experience.chapter2.title: The Formalisation Years
experience.chapter2.quote: It clarified something important: I wanted to build, not just coordinate.
experience.chapter2.image.caption: Building U/skillity – peer-to-peer learning platform
experience.chapter2.p1: Ireland was intense. Full-time business and marketing, but I found myself drawn to a computer science module I'd added. **Java clicked** in a way the business courses didn't. Five days of lectures, evenings and weekends at an Apple retail job to finance it. U/skillity continued remotely.
experience.chapter2.p2: After a year and a half, I discovered that acceptance to one EU university meant I could transfer anywhere in Europe. **CODE University** in Berlin was focused on interdisciplinary product development and applied learning. I applied, got in, and moved back home in 2018 to study **Product Management**.
experience.chapter2.p3: CODE was where things started connecting. The programme emphasised synthesis: how technology, design, business, and human needs intersect. I also needed to work, which led me to YPTOKEY, a startup building blockchain-based IoT access systems.
experience.chapter2.p4: I joined as a **Product Owner and Frontend Developer**, but quickly found myself translating. The CEO and CTO spoke different languages (business strategy vs technical architecture) and I could understand both. I built **React proof-of-concepts** for customers, explained blockchain to sales teams, bridged vision and implementation. First time I'd built something with code that mattered to a business outcome. Largely self-taught, drawing on Java foundations from Ireland and resources at CODE.
experience.chapter2.p5: When COVID hit in 2020, YPTOKEY faced financial pressure and I lost the role. I realised I missed programming more than product management. In early 2021, I took a Technical Project Manager role at **Data4Life**. The team was kind, but the work felt misaligned: startup culture inside a corporate structure, with people who didn't want that. It clarified something: **I wanted to build, not coordinate**.
experience.chapter2.p6: By mid-2021, I'd moved to **Freiheit.software** as a Frontend Developer. Remote work, travelling while coding, real enterprise applications with **React, Node.js, and TypeScript**. Then the team needed full-stack support. I got pulled into backend work and discovered I enjoyed it even more. Designing systems end-to-end, thinking about architecture, data flow, how pieces fit together.
experience.chapter2.p7: When Freiheit lost a client in late 2022 and had to let me go, I used one of their former customer contacts to start freelancing. After years of employment, I thought independence might be what I needed.
experience.chapter3.title: Seeking Depth
experience.chapter3.subtitle: 2023 - Present
experience.chapter3.quote: I want problems that take longer than an afternoon.
experience.chapter3.image.caption: The freelance reality – working from anywhere
experience.chapter3.p1: Since 2023 I've worked freelance, mostly on websites for artists and small businesses, owning each project from the first call to deployment. It made clear what I want next: **backend and systems work in a team**, with code review and problems that take longer than an afternoon.
experience.chapter3.p2: In 2025 I completed the **Advanced Web Development programme at Neue Fische**. Currently I'm in a six-month **AWS Cloud & DevOps program** (Terraform, Docker, CI/CD, AWS architecture), preparing for the AWS Solutions Architect Associate exam, through Q1 2027.
experience.chapter3.p3: On the side, I'm rebuilding **U/skillity** with NestJS, Next.js and PostgreSQL. The idea that passionate people teach best never left me.
experience.chapter3.p4: Sound, spaces, software – and lately wood again. I like building things that have to work in the real world.
experience.chapter3.lessons.title: What each stage taught me
experience.chapter3.lessons.1: **Audio engineering:** building a whole from separate components.
experience.chapter3.lessons.2: **Kultstätte Keller:** managing complexity and adapting to what emerges.
experience.chapter3.lessons.3: **Film sets:** working together under pressure and taking craft seriously.
experience.chapter3.lessons.4: **U/skillity:** I care about how people learn.
experience.chapter3.lessons.6: **Freiheit.software:** I love backend and systems work.
